title: Act when focal symptoms resolve
stem: A client's unilateral arm weakness and difficulty speaking resolve after ten minutes. They now want to resume routine activities. What is most appropriate?
options: Schedule a routine blood-pressure review.
Ask the client to keep a symptom diary.
Continue usual follow-up after a normal motor recheck.
Arrange urgent stroke or TIA assessment.
why: Risk-factor management matters, but it does not address the urgency of this new focal neurological episode.
A diary can supplement the history but should not delay urgent evaluation of a transient deficit.
Normal current strength does not negate the observed episode or establish that its cause is benign.
Transient focal deficits can signal a time-sensitive vascular event and short-term stroke risk despite resolution.
takeaway: Transient focal deficits can signal a time-sensitive vascular event and short-term stroke risk despite resolution.
learningObjective: Arrange urgent assessment for a transient focal neurological deficit despite apparent recovery.

title: Recognize a possible posterior circulation event
stem: A client suddenly develops severe imbalance, vomiting and double vision. Hand grasps remain equal. Which concern requires urgent assessment?
options: A posterior-circulation stroke.
Benign positional vertigo.
Medication-related dizziness.
Acute gastroenteritis.
why: Sudden diplopia and severe imbalance can reflect a posterior brain circulation event despite preserved hand strength.
Vertigo can cause nausea and imbalance, but new double vision raises concern for a central neurological process.
Medicines may cause dizziness, but the abrupt combination with diplopia requires urgent neurological evaluation.
Vomiting may occur with gastrointestinal illness, but it does not explain the new diplopia and severe balance disturbance.
takeaway: Sudden diplopia and severe imbalance can reflect a posterior brain circulation event despite preserved hand strength.
learningObjective: Consider stroke when sudden balance and coordination symptoms occur without typical arm weakness.

title: Escalate a thunderclap headache
stem: A client with occasional migraines reports a new headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds and feels unlike previous headaches. What is the priority?
options: Encourage rest in a dark, quiet room.
Arrange immediate emergency assessment.
Use the existing migraine rescue plan.
Arrange a same-week headache follow-up.
why: Comfort measures may reduce distress but do not assess a possible intracranial emergency.
Maximal-at-onset pain that differs from prior migraines requires investigation for an acute intracranial cause.
An established migraine plan does not establish that this qualitatively different onset has the same cause.
The abrupt warning pattern needs more urgent evaluation than an outpatient appointment later in the week.
takeaway: Maximal-at-onset pain that differs from prior migraines requires investigation for an acute intracranial cause.
learningObjective: Recognize an abrupt maximal-intensity headache as an emergency rather than assuming usual migraine.

title: Recognize delayed head-injury deterioration
stem: A client initially spoke normally after a head injury but is now increasingly difficult to arouse and repeatedly vomiting. What is appropriate?
options: Reduce stimulation and allow uninterrupted sleep.
Review discharge readiness from the original observations.
Activate urgent neurological reassessment.
Administer the prescribed antiemetic.
why: Rest does not explain or safely manage progressive loss of responsiveness after injury.
Earlier normal speech cannot establish discharge readiness after a new decline.
Progressive difficulty arousing the client and repeated vomiting after a head injury suggest evolving intracranial deterioration.
Symptom relief does not address declining consciousness; urgent neurological care should proceed.
takeaway: Progressive difficulty arousing the client and repeated vomiting after a head injury suggest evolving intracranial deterioration.
learningObjective: Interpret a decline after initial alertness as possible evolving intracranial injury.

title: Assess comprehension despite expressive aphasia
stem: After a stroke, a client has effortful, incomplete spoken phrases. They accurately follow two different spoken instructions that are not demonstrated and answer factual yes/no questions reliably. Which assessment description best fits?
options: Fluent language production with impaired comprehension.
Isolated dysarthria with intact word production.
Global language impairment affecting both expression and understanding.
Expressive language difficulty with relatively preserved comprehension.
why: The speech is not fluent, and the accurate responses argue against comprehension being the main demonstrated deficit.
Dysarthria affects motor articulation; incomplete effortful language formulation is different from simply slurred but otherwise appropriate speech.
The consistent comprehension demonstrated here does not support equally severe receptive and expressive impairment.
The client understands the unmodelled commands and questions but struggles to formulate speech; fuller language assessment is still needed.
takeaway: The client understands the unmodelled commands and questions but struggles to formulate speech; fuller language assessment is still needed.
learningObjective: Differentiate expressive language impairment from impaired comprehension and motor articulation using observed responses.

title: Identify neurological deterioration from baseline
stem: A client is under observation after an intracranial event. Which findings represent concerning changes from the documented baseline? Select all that apply.
options: An unchanged pupil difference documented before admission
The same longstanding hand tremor without functional change
New difficulty staying awake during assessment
New unilateral weakness compared with the previous examination
A pupil becomes newly larger and poorly reactive
why: A stable pre-existing asymmetry is less concerning than a new change.
An unchanged chronic finding does not by itself establish acute deterioration.
A declining level of consciousness can indicate worsening brain function.
A new focal deficit requires timely neurological assessment.
A new pupil change can indicate evolving intracranial compromise.
takeaway: A declining level of consciousness can indicate worsening brain function.
learningObjective: Select new neurological changes that warrant escalation rather than stable pre-existing findings.

title: Escalate a prolonged seizure
stem: A generalized seizure continues beyond the client's documented emergency rescue threshold. The nurse is competent and authorized to follow that plan. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Administer the prescribed rescue medicine according to the plan
Wait for spontaneous recovery before alerting the team
Give the next routine oral antiseizure tablet during convulsions
Restart timing each time limb movements briefly lessen
Activate the emergency response while supporting airway safety
why: The established threshold authorizes timely rescue treatment rather than continued waiting.
This delays the response specified for a prolonged seizure.
Oral administration is unsafe and does not substitute for the rescue route.
Brief fluctuation does not necessarily mark recovery or a new event.
Prolonged seizure activity needs prompt assistance and physiological support.
takeaway: Prolonged seizure activity needs prompt assistance and physiological support.
learningObjective: Activate emergency treatment when seizure duration exceeds the prescribed rescue threshold.

title: Recognize seizures without recovery
stem: A client has another convulsive seizure before regaining consciousness from the first. Which interpretation best guides care?
options: Routine postictal recovery.
Medication-related sleepiness.
A continuing seizure emergency.
Separate self-limited seizure events.
why: New convulsions during unconsciousness are not simply resolving postictal sleep.
Medication effects may influence arousal but do not adequately explain the repeated active convulsions.
Repeated convulsions without return to baseline require immediate escalation and support for ventilation and neurological safety.
The lack of recovery between events is a critical feature that increases urgency.
takeaway: Repeated convulsions without return to baseline require immediate escalation and support for ventilation and neurological safety.
learningObjective: Distinguish recurrent seizures without return to baseline from a single resolving postictal period.

title: Evaluate postictal recovery
stem: After a brief seizure, which findings support recovery toward baseline? Select all that apply.
options: The client becomes harder to arouse at each check
A new unilateral weakness persists on repeated checks
Another seizure begins before consciousness returns
Breathing is regular with a maintained airway
The client becomes progressively more responsive and oriented
why: Progressive loss of responsiveness needs urgent reassessment.
A persistent focal change warrants neurological evaluation rather than assumed routine recovery.
Recurrence without recovery indicates a seizure emergency.
Stable ventilation is necessary during the recovery period.
Improvement over serial assessments supports resolving postictal effects.
takeaway: Stable ventilation is necessary during the recovery period.
learningObjective: Use airway status and improving mentation to distinguish recovery from continuing deterioration.

title: Document a possible focal seizure
stem: A client abruptly stops responding during conversation, makes repetitive chewing movements for about one minute and later cannot recall it. Which report best preserves the clinically important event?
options: Abrupt one-minute episode of chewing and absent response; client later reports amnesia.
One-minute refusal to answer with chewing; client later unable to explain the behaviour.
One-minute episode of chewing and anxiety; client then returned to usual conversation.
Client conversing normally after a brief pause; no current memory of the discussion.
why: This records onset, behaviour, responsiveness, duration and recovery information without assigning intent, supporting seizure assessment.
Calling the episode refusal assumes intent despite sudden unresponsiveness and amnesia.
This adds an unestablished emotional interpretation and omits the loss of responsiveness and recall.
The later state alone understates the stereotyped movements and unresponsiveness during the event.
takeaway: This records onset, behaviour, responsiveness, duration and recovery information without assigning intent, supporting seizure assessment.
learningObjective: Describe observed behaviour and recovery without assuming deliberate nonparticipation.

title: Recognize bulbar weakness in myasthenia
stem: A client with myasthenia gravis is being reassessed. Which changes require prompt evaluation for a possible crisis? Select all that apply.
options: The usual mild evening eyelid droop is unchanged
Hand strength matches the documented baseline
The voice becomes weak and speech trails off after a few words
The cough becomes weak and saliva is difficult to clear
Breathing becomes shallow with visible fatigue
why: An established stable ocular symptom is less urgent than new bulbar or respiratory decline.
Unchanged limb strength does not itself indicate new crisis.
Fatiguing bulbar function can accompany significant neuromuscular weakness.
Reduced clearance threatens airway protection.
Respiratory muscle weakness can lead to ventilatory failure.
takeaway: Fatiguing bulbar function can accompany significant neuromuscular weakness.
learningObjective: Identify changes suggesting airway-protection or respiratory risk during myasthenia gravis.

title: Assess ventilation during Guillain-Barré progression
stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome has spreading weakness and difficulty taking a deep breath, while saturation remains 97%. Which ordered assessment most directly helps detect declining respiratory muscle function?
options: Auscultation of the lung fields.
A one-minute respiratory-rate count.
Serial forced vital-capacity measurements.
Repeat conventional pulse-oximetry readings.
why: Breath sounds may be clear despite respiratory muscle failure, so auscultation is less direct for this question.
Rate is important but may not reveal declining depth or reserve as directly as serial lung-volume measurements.
A falling vital capacity can identify declining ventilatory reserve before routine saturation falls; trained staff perform and report the ordered assessment.
Oximetry remains useful but measures oxygenation rather than respiratory muscle strength.
takeaway: A falling vital capacity can identify declining ventilatory reserve before routine saturation falls; trained staff perform and report the ordered assessment.
learningObjective: Select an ordered respiratory-function measure that can detect declining ventilatory reserve in Guillain-Barré syndrome.

title: Recognize autonomic instability with Guillain-Barré
stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome develops marked fluctuations in pulse and blood pressure. Which nursing responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use one normal reading to return to the previous observation plan.
Report possible autonomic involvement promptly.
Continue the ordered cardiac and blood-pressure monitoring.
Treat the pressure rises as episodes of pain.
Reduce measurements to standard once-per-shift checks.
why: Intermittent normalization does not establish resolution of autonomic episodes.
Guillain-Barré syndrome can disrupt autonomic control and produce clinically important pulse and pressure instability.
Trends help detect intermittent dysrhythmias and pressure changes that a single normal reading can miss.
Pain can affect pressure, but marked fluctuations during this illness warrant assessment for dysautonomia.
Routine intervals may miss the current instability and would depart from the ordered monitoring plan.
takeaway: Guillain-Barré syndrome can disrupt autonomic control and produce clinically important pulse and pressure instability.
learningObjective: Identify cardiovascular changes requiring monitoring during acute peripheral nerve dysfunction.

title: Investigate a reversible trigger of worsening weakness
stem: A client with multiple sclerosis develops worse weakness during fever and urinary symptoms. Which nursing actions are indicated now? Select all that apply.
options: Record the episode as permanent disease progression.
Schedule routine strengthening therapy.
Recheck neurological function after the antipyretic has taken effect.
Compare the neurological findings with the established baseline.
Assess for infection and obtain ordered specimens.
why: A transient illness-related worsening is possible, and permanence cannot be established from this episode.
Rehabilitation may help later, but current weakness with infection symptoms requires acute assessment.
A later comparison may be useful, but an initial assessment and report should not wait for fever reduction.
The degree and nature of the change guide urgency; a reversible trigger must not obscure a new neurological problem.
Fever and infection can worsen existing symptoms, so the acute trigger needs evaluation.
takeaway: The degree and nature of the change guide urgency; a reversible trigger must not obscure a new neurological problem.
learningObjective: Assess fever and infection before attributing all new multiple-sclerosis symptoms to progression.

title: Respond to autonomic dysreflexia
stem: A client with a high spinal cord injury develops a pounding headache, flushing and blood pressure far above baseline. The urinary catheter tubing is kinked. What is appropriate?
options: Lay the client flat to support cerebral perfusion.
Initiate the dysreflexia protocol and relieve the visible catheter kink.
Repeat the pressure after scheduled bladder care.
Administer the prescribed headache analgesic.
why: Flat positioning may worsen the hypertensive response; upright positioning is generally part of the immediate protocol.
The pattern suggests autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder distension; the protocol includes prompt upright positioning, trigger relief and continued pressure monitoring.
The current symptomatic hypertension and visible kink need immediate attention rather than the routine schedule.
Pain relief does not remove the triggering distension or address the dangerous blood-pressure rise.
takeaway: The pattern suggests autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder distension; the protocol includes prompt upright positioning, trigger relief and continued pressure monitoring.
learningObjective: Recognize a hypertensive emergency pattern after high spinal injury and address triggers under protocol.

title: Recognize cauda equina warning symptoms
stem: A client with back pain develops urinary retention and numbness around the perineum. Which concern requires urgent evaluation?
options: Uncomplicated lumbar muscle strain.
Distal peripheral neuropathy.
Cauda equina compression.
Isolated lower urinary obstruction.
why: A simple strain does not adequately explain new bladder dysfunction or saddle sensory change.
Typical distal neuropathy does not fit the acute saddle-and-bladder pattern as well as a compressive spinal process.
New saddle sensory change and bladder dysfunction suggest compromised sacral nerve function requiring time-sensitive assessment.
Obstruction may explain retention but does not explain the new perineal sensory loss associated with back pain.
takeaway: New saddle sensory change and bladder dysfunction suggest compromised sacral nerve function requiring time-sensitive assessment.
learningObjective: Escalate new bladder dysfunction and saddle sensory loss with back pain.

title: Escalate new deficits after spinal surgery
stem: Four hours after lumbar spinal surgery, which new report requires immediate escalation? All findings are compared with the documented recovery-room baseline.
options: Incisional pain returns as the prescribed analgesic interval ends.
The unchanged preoperative toe numbness is still present.
Mild nausea improves after the prescribed antiemetic.
Both legs are newly weak, and bladder control has been lost.
why: Recurrent incisional pain requires treatment assessment, but it is less urgent than new neurological loss.
A stable pre-existing sensory deficit should be monitored but is not the new emergency finding.
A responding common postoperative symptom does not carry the urgency of acute motor and bladder dysfunction.
Acute bilateral motor and bladder change may indicate a compressive or other surgical complication requiring immediate assessment.
takeaway: Acute bilateral motor and bladder change may indicate a compressive or other surgical complication requiring immediate assessment.
learningObjective: Recognize acute postoperative neurological change as a possible compressive complication.

title: Prioritize suspected meningitis deterioration
stem: A client has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and increasing difficulty staying awake. Which concern best explains the need for urgent physiological assessment?
options: Central nervous system infection.
A familiar migraine episode.
A tension-type headache.
An uncomplicated viral upper-respiratory illness.
why: The fever, meningeal symptoms and altered consciousness suggest meningitis or another CNS infection requiring urgent assessment and support.
Migraine may cause headache and nausea, but fever, neck stiffness and declining arousal require a different urgent evaluation.
Tension headache does not adequately explain systemic illness or progressive impaired consciousness.
The neurological and meningeal findings make this more concerning than a routine upper-respiratory infection.
takeaway: The fever, meningeal symptoms and altered consciousness suggest meningitis or another CNS infection requiring urgent assessment and support.
learningObjective: Recognize fever with meningeal and consciousness changes as an urgent physiological problem.

title: Protect a possible CSF leak
stem: After head trauma, a client develops new clear nasal drainage. A skull-base injury is suspected. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Pack the nostril tightly to stop the fluid
Insert nasal suction to determine the drainage source
Treat a bedside glucose strip as definitive proof of CSF
Report the drainage and follow the diagnostic collection plan
Discourage nose blowing while awaiting assessment
why: Packing can obstruct drainage and introduce trauma or infection.
Nasal instrumentation may be hazardous with suspected skull-base injury.
A nonspecific bedside glucose result cannot confirm the diagnosis.
The team needs to evaluate a possible cerebrospinal-fluid leak.
Increased nasal pressure may worsen leakage or introduce complications.
takeaway: The team needs to evaluate a possible cerebrospinal-fluid leak.
learningObjective: Avoid obstructing or traumatizing new clear nasal drainage after head injury.

title: Recognize possible shunt malfunction
stem: A child with a ventricular shunt develops repeated vomiting, headache and unusual sleepiness. The caregiver says this is not the child's usual behaviour. What is appropriate?
options: Assess for visible swelling along the shunt tract.
Begin an oral rehydration trial for the vomiting.
Arrange urgent neurological and shunt assessment.
Treat the vomiting as gastroenteritis.
why: The tract should be examined, but an absence of swelling would not exclude obstruction or internal malfunction.
Hydration does not resolve the need to assess the associated headache and altered alertness urgently.
Headache, vomiting and unusual sleepiness may reflect impaired CSF drainage and raised intracranial pressure.
Another illness is possible, but the shunt history and neurological change require prompt assessment for malfunction.
takeaway: Headache, vomiting and unusual sleepiness may reflect impaired CSF drainage and raised intracranial pressure.
learningObjective: Escalate new vomiting and neurological decline in a child with a cerebrospinal-fluid shunt.

title: Interpret an infant's neurological warning pattern
stem: An infant is febrile, feeds poorly and has a bulging fontanelle while calm and upright. What is the best response?
options: Repeat feeding after the fever medicine takes effect.
Offer smaller, more frequent feeds.
Repeat the fontanelle assessment while the infant is crying.
Arrange urgent assessment for possible intracranial disease.
why: Feeding support does not address the current neurological warning finding and should not delay assessment.
This may help some feeding problems, but the systemic and fontanelle findings require broader urgent evaluation.
Crying can transiently increase fullness and is less informative than the already abnormal calm, upright finding.
Persistent bulging while calm and upright with fever and poor feeding is concerning for infection or increased pressure.
takeaway: Persistent bulging while calm and upright with fever and poor feeding is concerning for infection or increased pressure.
learningObjective: Distinguish a concerning bulging fontanelle pattern from transient fullness during crying.

title: Consider an organic cause of acute behavioural change
stem: A previously independent adult develops fever, new bizarre behaviour and a first seizure. What should guide initial care?
options: Arrange urgent medical assessment for an acute brain or systemic process.
Request a routine psychiatric review of the behaviour.
Use de-escalation and environmental support.
Observe for a possible panic-related episode.
why: Fever and a first seizure with new behavioural change require urgent physiological evaluation regardless of the unusual behaviour.
Psychiatric input may become relevant, but the fever and first seizure make medical assessment the initial priority.
These can support safety during care but do not replace assessment of the underlying physiological emergency.
Panic does not adequately explain fever and a first seizure, and observation alone could delay essential treatment.
takeaway: Fever and a first seizure with new behavioural change require urgent physiological evaluation regardless of the unusual behaviour.
learningObjective: Identify fever and new seizures as cues requiring medical assessment of behavioural change.

title: Escalate transient monocular vision loss
stem: A client reports a painless dark curtain over one eye for several minutes that has now resolved. What is appropriate?
options: Track future episodes in a home symptom diary.
Arrange urgent vascular and ophthalmic assessment.
Arrange routine cardiovascular-risk follow-up.
Book a routine refraction appointment.
why: Recording details can help clinicians, but waiting for recurrence would delay the current evaluation.
A transient monocular curtain may reflect retinal ischemia or another serious process even after vision returns.
Long-term risk reduction matters, but it does not replace urgent evaluation of this possible ischemic warning episode.
Refractive error does not explain the abrupt, transient dark curtain pattern.
takeaway: A transient monocular curtain may reflect retinal ischemia or another serious process even after vision returns.
learningObjective: Recognize sudden one-eye visual loss as requiring urgent vascular and ophthalmic assessment.

title: Recognize acute angle-closure symptoms
stem: A client develops sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision with halos, headache and vomiting. Which complication is most concerning?
options: Conjunctivitis.
Retinal detachment.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Migraine.
why: Conjunctivitis usually causes surface irritation or discharge rather than this severe painful visual loss and vomiting pattern.
Detachment more often causes painless flashes, floaters or a field curtain; this painful syndrome favours angle closure.
The painful visual and systemic pattern can indicate rapidly elevated intraocular pressure requiring emergency eye assessment.
Migraine can cause headache and visual symptoms, but severe ocular pain with halos requires consideration of an eye-pressure emergency.
takeaway: The painful visual and systemic pattern can indicate rapidly elevated intraocular pressure requiring emergency eye assessment.
learningObjective: Identify an acute painful visual-disturbance pattern requiring emergency eye assessment.

title: Respond to retinal-detachment warning symptoms
stem: A client develops new flashes, many floaters and a shadow spreading across one eye's vision, without pain. What is most appropriate?
options: Arrange a routine refraction appointment next month
Wait for redness or eye pain to confirm severity
Advise screen rest as the main treatment
Urgent ophthalmic assessment for possible retinal detachment
why: A refractive problem does not explain this acute retinal warning pattern.
Retinal detachment may remain painless and externally quiet.
Rest does not reattach a threatened retina or replace urgent assessment.
Retinal separation can threaten vision despite painless symptoms.
takeaway: Retinal separation can threaten vision despite painless symptoms.
learningObjective: Escalate new flashes, floaters and a visual-field curtain despite absent pain.

title: Escalate hyperkalemia with ECG changes
stem: A client with acute kidney injury has potassium 6.8 mmol/L, reference 3.5–5.0, and new ECG changes. What is the priority?
options: Activate urgent treatment and cardiac monitoring under protocol.
Repeat the potassium sample.
Review dietary potassium sources.
Assess the client's muscle strength.
why: Potassium 6.8 mmol/L with ECG changes threatens cardiac stability and needs immediate protocol-based response.
A repeat may be appropriate during care, but the existing electrical changes mean treatment must not wait for confirmation.
Diet contributes to later management but does not address the immediate dysrhythmia risk.
Neuromuscular findings are relevant, but cardiac toxicity may be severe even without marked weakness.
takeaway: Potassium 6.8 mmol/L with ECG changes threatens cardiac stability and needs immediate protocol-based response.
learningObjective: Prioritize cardiac protection and protocol treatment when severe hyperkalemia has electrical effects.

title: Review a hemolyzed potassium result
stem: A stable client's unexpectedly high potassium result is flagged as heavily hemolyzed. There are no new symptoms or ECG changes. What is appropriate?
options: Request potassium-lowering treatment based on the single reported value.
Report the result and arrange a fresh atraumatic sample promptly.
Ask the laboratory to reanalyse the same hemolyzed specimen.
Arrange review at the next routine clinic blood draw.
why: In this stable context, possible specimen error should be urgently clarified to avoid harmful unnecessary correction; hemolysis does not itself prove potassium is normal.
Hemolysis may falsely increase potassium; urgent redraw helps resolve the result while the team considers the clinical picture.
Repeating analysis of the damaged sample may reproduce the same preanalytical distortion.
The potentially critical result needs timely resolution rather than waiting for routine follow-up.
takeaway: Hemolysis may falsely increase potassium; urgent redraw helps resolve the result while the team considers the clinical picture.
learningObjective: Resolve a potentially spurious potassium result without dismissing a critical value.

title: Interpret hypokalemia with neuromuscular changes
stem: A client with prolonged vomiting has potassium 2.7 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0), weakness and reduced bowel activity. Which complications are consistent with this disturbance? Select all that apply.
options: Water retention from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone release.
Cardiac rhythm instability.
Further skeletal-muscle weakness.
Gastrointestinal hypomotility or ileus.
Carpopedal spasm from increased neuromuscular excitability.
why: SIADH is not an expected consequence of potassium depletion; it involves a different water-regulation disturbance.
Marked potassium depletion alters cardiac electrical activity and can cause dangerous dysrhythmias.
Low potassium can impair muscle function, potentially including respiratory muscles when severe.
The reduced bowel activity may reflect electrolyte-related loss of smooth-muscle function.
This pattern is more characteristic of low ionized calcium than the flaccid weakness of hypokalemia.
takeaway: Marked potassium depletion alters cardiac electrical activity and can cause dangerous dysrhythmias.
learningObjective: Connect marked potassium depletion with weakness, bowel slowing and rhythm risk.

title: Recognize symptomatic hypocalcemia after neck surgery
stem: After thyroid surgery, a client develops tingling around the mouth and hand spasms. Which postoperative complication is most concerning?
options: An expanding neck hematoma.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
A surgical-wound infection.
Hypocalcemia with tetany.
why: A hematoma can threaten the airway but more typically causes local swelling or pressure, not the characteristic tingling and hand spasms described.
This is more likely to produce voice changes or airway issues than generalized neuromuscular irritability.
Infection does not best explain the acute perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm pattern.
Perioral paresthesia and spasms suggest low calcium; promptly assess airway symptoms and arrange calcium evaluation and treatment review.
takeaway: Perioral paresthesia and spasms suggest low calcium; promptly assess airway symptoms and arrange calcium evaluation and treatment review.
learningObjective: Escalate neuromuscular irritability suggesting low calcium after thyroid surgery.

title: Recognize concurrent magnesium depletion
stem: After prolonged diarrhea has stopped, potassium remains 2.9 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) despite prescribed replacement. Magnesium is 0.40 mmol/L (reference 0.70–1.00). There is no new vomiting, diuresis, insulin treatment or large fluid infusion. Which mechanism should the nurse raise with the team?
options: Magnesium depletion promoting continued renal potassium loss.
Dilution of potassium by a recent large fluid load.
A recent insulin-induced shift of potassium into cells.
Inadequate replacement for a newly increasing gastrointestinal loss.
why: Low magnesium can make potassium difficult to correct; the identified deficit warrants a coordinated replacement and monitoring plan.
The history does not include the fluid exposure needed to support dilution as the main explanation.
Insulin can shift potassium, but there has been no recent insulin treatment in this case.
The diarrhea has stopped and no new losses are reported; the low magnesium is the demonstrated contributor that needs attention.
takeaway: Low magnesium can make potassium difficult to correct; the identified deficit warrants a coordinated replacement and monitoring plan.
learningObjective: Consider magnesium when potassium remains low despite prescribed replacement.

title: Respond to a seizure with severe hyponatremia
stem: A client with sodium 116 mmol/L, reference 135–145, develops a seizure. What is the priority after immediate airway and injury protection begins?
options: Collect a complete fluid-intake history.
Activate emergency protocol treatment for symptomatic hyponatremia.
Obtain a repeat sodium sample.
Prepare the routine oral sodium supplement.
why: The history will help identify the cause, but emergency treatment takes priority over completing it.
A seizure with sodium 116 mmol/L is a neurological emergency requiring controlled correction and close monitoring.
Verification may occur during care, but it should not delay treatment of the current severe symptomatic disturbance.
Routine oral replacement is not an adequate immediate response to seizure-related severe hyponatremia.
takeaway: A seizure with sodium 116 mmol/L is a neurological emergency requiring controlled correction and close monitoring.
learningObjective: Treat symptomatic severe sodium disturbance as an emergency requiring controlled correction.

title: Evaluate hypernatremia treatment safely
stem: A dehydrated older adult receives a prescribed controlled correction plan for marked hypernatremia. Which changes require prompt review during treatment? Select all that apply.
options: New crackles with increasing oxygen requirement.
A sodium fall faster than the maximum rate stated in the order.
Thirst eases while sodium changes within the ordered rate.
Urine output improves with stable pressure and clear lung sounds.
New headache and decreasing alertness during the infusion.
why: Emerging congestion suggests poor fluid tolerance and requires review of the current plan.
The measured trend exceeds this client's controlled correction plan and requires prompt action under protocol.
This is consistent with a response but does not eliminate the need for ongoing sodium and neurological monitoring.
These findings can support improved hydration when considered with the full trend rather than indicating a new treatment complication.
Neurological deterioration can signal an unsafe shift or another complication and warrants immediate reassessment.
takeaway: Neurological deterioration can signal an unsafe shift or another complication and warrants immediate reassessment.
learningObjective: Monitor neurological and fluid trends during prescribed controlled correction of hypernatremia.

title: Anticipate potassium changes during DKA treatment
stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis begins prescribed insulin and fluids. Initial potassium was high, but it is now falling. What explains the monitoring need?
options: Insulin moves potassium from cells into the blood.
Insulin removes potassium directly through the kidneys.
The initial high concentration shows adequate total potassium reserves.
Insulin moves potassium into cells while total stores may be depleted.
why: The relevant insulin effect is movement into cells, which can lower the measured serum level.
Insulin primarily redistributes potassium; removal depends on kidney function or other elimination therapy.
Distribution changes can raise serum potassium despite substantial losses from the body.
An initially high serum concentration can mask a whole-body potassium deficit during DKA.
takeaway: An initially high serum concentration can mask a whole-body potassium deficit during DKA.
learningObjective: Explain why potassium may fall during insulin treatment despite an initially normal or high value.

title: Continue DKA care after glucose improves
stem: A client remains on an IV DKA protocol. Glucose approaches the protocol target, but blood ketones and acidosis persist. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Continue protocol insulin with prescribed glucose-containing fluid as indicated.
Stop insulin after the glucose target is reached.
Determine resolution from the increased urine output.
Resume routine meals and the usual subcutaneous regimen.
why: Insulin may still be needed to clear ketosis while glucose-containing fluid protects against hypoglycemia.
Glucose improvement alone does not establish resolution of ketoacidosis.
Improved output may reflect resuscitation but does not show that ketones and acidosis have cleared.
Transition requires the protocol's metabolic and clinical criteria, not simply a glucose target.
takeaway: Insulin may still be needed to clear ketosis while glucose-containing fluid protects against hypoglycemia.
learningObjective: Distinguish improvement in glucose from resolution of ketoacidosis.

title: Recognize severe hyperosmolar illness without ketones
stem: An older adult with type 2 diabetes is confused and profoundly dehydrated. Glucose is 42 mmol/L, calculated serum osmolality 338 mOsm/kg (reference 275–295), pH 7.36 (reference 7.35–7.45), and blood ketones are minimally elevated. Which concern best fits?
options: Uncomplicated dehydration from reduced intake.
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.
Diabetic ketoacidosis as the dominant disturbance.
Hypoglycemia with neurological impairment.
why: The severity of hyperglycemia, osmolality and neurological change exceeds uncomplicated dehydration and requires urgent metabolic management.
Marked hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration with little acidosis support this emergency; assess for overlap rather than assuming mixed disease is impossible.
DKA usually includes significant ketosis and metabolic acidosis, which are not the dominant findings here.
The measured glucose is markedly elevated, not low.
takeaway: Marked hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration with little acidosis support this emergency; assess for overlap rather than assuming mixed disease is impossible.
learningObjective: Identify profound dehydration and neurological change as serious despite minimal ketosis.

title: Recognize diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery
stem: After pituitary surgery, a client passes large amounts of very dilute urine and becomes increasingly thirsty; sodium rises above range. What is appropriate?
options: Review whether diuretics were given perioperatively.
Continue the usual postoperative fluid allowance.
Promptly assess fluid balance and report possible diabetes insipidus.
Compare today's weight with yesterday's.
why: Medication history matters, but the surgical context and rising sodium still require prompt assessment for diabetes insipidus.
The new excessive losses may require a revised prescribed plan; the earlier allowance may no longer match current needs.
Large dilute output with rising sodium after pituitary surgery suggests impaired antidiuretic function and potentially rapid free-water loss.
Weight is useful but a daily comparison does not replace response to rapid ongoing losses.
takeaway: Large dilute output with rising sodium after pituitary surgery suggests impaired antidiuretic function and potentially rapid free-water loss.
learningObjective: Connect high dilute urine output and rising sodium with impaired antidiuretic function.

title: Apply a prescribed SIADH fluid limit
stem: A client with SIADH has an individualized total daily fluid allowance. Which nursing practices help account for that allowance accurately? Select all that apply.
options: Allocate fluid across meals, medication administration and shifts.
Record plain water separately and exclude milk from the total.
Count IV medication diluents in a separate total outside the allowance.
Use the amount requested for thirst as the next shift's allocation.
Include drinks, ice and other fluid sources specified in the plan.
why: A shared allocation helps prevent accidental excess while meeting necessary care needs.
Milk still supplies fluid, so omitting it would undercount intake.
When the order concerns total intake, prescribed IV carriers must be accounted for unless the plan explicitly says otherwise.
Thirst does not determine the authorized total or establish that the sodium disturbance has resolved.
Foods and ice that become liquid may contribute to intake; use the prescribed counting method.
takeaway: Foods and ice that become liquid may contribute to intake; use the prescribed counting method.
learningObjective: Account for all fluid sources when carrying out an individualized SIADH restriction.

title: Recognize thyroid storm physiology
stem: A client with poorly controlled hyperthyroidism develops a temperature of 40.1°C, pulse 152/minute, agitation and diarrhea during an infection. Which concern most urgently guides escalation?
options: Thyroid storm.
Uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis.
Infection without endocrine decompensation.
Panic-related symptoms.
why: Severe hyperthermia, tachycardia and neurological and gastrointestinal changes suggest acute endocrine decompensation requiring emergency care.
The extreme multisystem deterioration goes beyond stable excess-thyroid symptoms and requires emergency assessment.
Infection may be the trigger and needs treatment, but the known hyperthyroidism and severe pattern also require assessment for storm.
Panic can cause tachycardia and distress but does not adequately explain this high fever and systemic illness.
takeaway: Severe hyperthermia, tachycardia and neurological and gastrointestinal changes suggest acute endocrine decompensation requiring emergency care.
learningObjective: Escalate extreme hypermetabolic and neurological findings in a client with hyperthyroidism.

title: Recognize severe hypothyroid decompensation
stem: A client with untreated hypothyroidism becomes hypothermic, bradycardic and difficult to arouse with slow breathing. What is appropriate?
options: Reconcile the missed thyroid medication doses.
Activate emergency support for ventilation.
Begin the prescribed gradual warming measures.
Obtain the ordered thyroid laboratory samples.
why: The history helps subsequent management but does not address the current ventilatory threat.
Slow breathing and impaired arousal threaten immediate physiological safety in severe hypothyroid decompensation.
Warming is relevant, but it should not displace urgent support for depressed ventilation.
Tests assist confirmation but must not delay response to reduced consciousness and breathing.
takeaway: Slow breathing and impaired arousal threaten immediate physiological safety in severe hypothyroid decompensation.
learningObjective: Identify hypothermia, reduced ventilation and altered consciousness as an endocrine emergency pattern.

title: Identify an adrenal-crisis pattern
stem: A client with primary adrenal insufficiency has vomited their prescribed steroid doses for two days. They are profoundly weak, blood pressure is 78/46 mmHg, sodium 124 mmol/L (reference 135–145), potassium 5.9 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) and glucose 3.4 mmol/L. Which concern best directs urgent escalation?
options: Diabetic ketoacidosis.
Thyroid storm.
Adrenal crisis.
Septic shock as the sole explanation.
why: The low glucose and established adrenal history do not fit typical DKA; further evaluation may be needed but adrenal crisis is the key concern.
The supplied steroid interruption, low glucose and electrolyte pattern point toward adrenal failure rather than severe thyroid excess.
Missed steroid replacement with hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and low glucose supports acute adrenal decompensation requiring urgent replacement and circulation support.
Infection may precipitate or coexist with crisis, but it does not remove the immediate significance of failed steroid replacement and this endocrine pattern.
takeaway: Missed steroid replacement with hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and low glucose supports acute adrenal decompensation requiring urgent replacement and circulation support.
learningObjective: Integrate known adrenal insufficiency with hypotension and electrolyte findings during acute illness.

title: Assess sudden loss of catheter drainage
stem: A catheterized client develops suprapubic discomfort and no drainage after repositioning. Blood pressure is stable. What is the best first action?
options: Request an intravenous fluid bolus.
Obtain renal-function blood tests.
Encourage oral fluid intake.
Inspect the catheter tubing and drainage system.
why: Fluid does not correct obstructed drainage and may increase bladder distension.
Laboratory assessment may become relevant, but the immediate mechanical cause can be checked at the bedside.
Increasing intake does not resolve a kinked or blocked drainage pathway and could prolong discomfort.
The positional timing and suprapubic discomfort suggest a potentially reversible obstruction that should be checked first.
takeaway: The positional timing and suprapubic discomfort suggest a potentially reversible obstruction that should be checked first.
learningObjective: Check reversible drainage obstruction before assuming all low output reflects renal failure.

title: Monitor after relief of urinary obstruction
stem: After urinary obstruction is relieved, output is 450–600 mL/hour for four hours. The nurse is monitoring for post-obstructive fluid and electrolyte loss. Which additional findings require prompt review? Select all that apply.
options: Potassium falls to 2.9 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0).
Suprapubic discomfort resolves after drainage begins.
Pulse and blood pressure remain at the documented baseline.
A repeat sodium remains 140 mmol/L (reference 135–145).
Blood pressure falls from 128/76 to 94/58 mmHg with new dizziness.
why: Marked diuresis can deplete electrolytes; this low value needs an authorized replacement and monitoring plan.
Relief of retention discomfort is an expected improvement, although it does not establish safe fluid balance.
Stable measurements are reassuring at that time but do not remove the need to continue trending them.
A stable in-range value is not itself a new complication, although further losses can change it.
High ongoing output with falling pressure and symptoms suggests clinically important volume loss.
takeaway: High ongoing output with falling pressure and symptoms suggests clinically important volume loss.
learningObjective: Recognize fluid and electrolyte risks when marked diuresis follows obstruction relief.

title: Recognize possible dialysis-associated peritonitis
stem: A client receiving peritoneal dialysis has new abdominal pain and cloudy effluent. What is most appropriate?
options: Repeat the next exchange and compare its clarity.
Contact the dialysis team and follow the aseptic specimen plan.
Give the usual constipation advice.
Discard the drained bag through the usual disposal route.
why: Waiting for another exchange could delay treatment; the current symptoms already warrant prompt contact.
New cloudy effluent with abdominal pain suggests peritonitis requiring prompt investigation and treatment.
Constipation can occur with dialysis but does not adequately explain away the current infectious warning pattern.
The current effluent may be needed for diagnostic sampling according to the team protocol.
takeaway: New cloudy effluent with abdominal pain suggests peritonitis requiring prompt investigation and treatment.
learningObjective: Escalate cloudy peritoneal effluent with abdominal symptoms while preserving aseptic sampling.

title: Report loss of fistula flow signs
stem: An established arteriovenous fistula had a palpable thrill yesterday. Today neither a thrill nor a bruit is found after careful reassessment. What is appropriate?
options: Arrange assessment at the next routine access appointment.
Review recent oral fluid intake to estimate dehydration.
Promptly contact the dialysis team about possible access failure.
Ask the client to perform hand exercises and reassess afterward.
why: Delay may reduce the opportunity for access preservation when flow is newly absent.
Volume status can affect flow, but the absent thrill and bruit still require prompt access assessment.
New absent flow signs may indicate thrombosis or severe obstruction; timely assessment can help preserve the access.
Exercise does not reliably restore an acutely thrombosed access and should not delay reporting the absent flow signs.
takeaway: New absent flow signs may indicate thrombosis or severe obstruction; timely assessment can help preserve the access.
learningObjective: Recognize absent fistula vibration as a possible access problem requiring prompt review.

title: Escalate neurological change during initial dialysis
stem: Ninety minutes into a first hemodialysis treatment, a client develops worsening headache, vomiting and confusion. Blood pressure is 132/78 mmHg, close to baseline, and capillary glucose is 6.4 mmol/L. Which concern should be raised immediately with the dialysis team?
options: Hypoglycemia from the treatment.
Cerebral hypoperfusion from dialysis-related hypotension.
Expected fatigue from starting dialysis.
Dialysis disequilibrium or another acute solute-shift complication.
why: The current measured glucose does not support hypoglycemia as the explanation for this decline.
This can cause symptoms, but the stable current pressure provides less support than the new neurological pattern during first treatment.
Fatigue can occur, but escalating headache, vomiting and confusion must not be treated as routine adaptation.
New neurological symptoms during an initial treatment warrant immediate reassessment for disequilibrium and other causes; the nurse does not make a definitive diagnosis.
takeaway: New neurological symptoms during an initial treatment warrant immediate reassessment for disequilibrium and other causes; the nurse does not make a definitive diagnosis.
learningObjective: Recognize acute neurological symptoms during dialysis as requiring immediate treatment-team assessment.

title: Recognize a febrile stone complication
stem: A client with a known ureteric stone develops fever, chills and worsening flank pain despite analgesia. What is the priority?
options: Arrange urgent assessment for infection with possible obstruction.
Increase oral fluids to encourage stone passage.
Continue straining each void for the stone.
Reassess pain after the next prescribed analgesic dose.
why: Fever and chills with a stone and worsening flank pain raise concern for an infected obstructed system that may need urgent drainage.
Routine passage advice does not treat a potentially infected obstruction.
Straining may help identify passage but does not address the current systemic infection signs.
Pain response cannot establish that infection or obstruction is resolving, so clinical review should proceed now.
takeaway: Fever and chills with a stone and worsening flank pain raise concern for an infected obstructed system that may need urgent drainage.
learningObjective: Escalate systemic infection cues in a client with possible urinary obstruction.

title: Recognize nephritic fluid consequences
stem: A young adult has cola-coloured urine, new facial puffiness, reduced urine output and hypertension after a recent infection. What concern should be reported?
options: A ureteric stone.
Acute glomerular disease with fluid retention.
A lower urinary tract infection.
Dehydration from the recent illness.
why: A stone can cause hematuria, but the diffuse retention findings without a described colicky pain pattern favour glomerular involvement.
Cola urine, oliguria, edema and hypertension after infection form a concerning renal glomerular pattern requiring assessment.
Lower infection may change urine appearance but does not best explain the edema, hypertension and reduced filtration pattern.
Dehydration can darken urine, but new edema and hypertension support retention rather than simple volume loss.
takeaway: Cola urine, oliguria, edema and hypertension after infection form a concerning renal glomerular pattern requiring assessment.
learningObjective: Connect hematuria with edema and hypertension to a possible acute renal process.

title: Monitor renal complications after rhabdomyolysis
stem: A client with confirmed rhabdomyolysis after a crush injury receives prescribed treatment. Which trends require prompt reporting? Select all that apply.
options: Temperature remains normal during serial observations.
Urine output falls while creatinine rises.
Potassium rises above range with new rhythm changes.
Muscle pain decreases with prescribed analgesia.
Urine becomes lighter while output remains adequate.
why: Normal temperature is not a new complication and does not exclude rhabdomyolysis-related kidney injury.
This may indicate evolving acute kidney injury from muscle-breakdown products or other contributors.
Released intracellular potassium can create an immediate dysrhythmia risk requiring urgent response.
Pain improvement is beneficial but does not establish that renal or electrolyte risks have resolved.
This can be a favourable trend but should be interpreted with renal function and electrolytes.
takeaway: This may indicate evolving acute kidney injury from muscle-breakdown products or other contributors.
learningObjective: Select kidney and electrolyte monitoring after major muscle injury.

title: Recognize losses during the diuretic recovery phase
stem: During recovery from acute kidney injury, urine output increases substantially while creatinine is still above baseline. What is appropriate?
options: Return to routine once-per-shift balance checks.
Restore the previous medication schedule.
Teach the usual maintenance fluid intake as the current plan.
Continue close fluid-balance and electrolyte monitoring.
why: The substantial ongoing losses may require closer monitoring than routine stable-client observations.
Clearance may remain impaired while creatinine is above baseline; dose review is still needed.
A routine amount may not match the diuretic-phase losses; replacement needs an individualized prescribed plan.
High output can precede full recovery of concentration and electrolyte regulation, so losses still require assessment.
takeaway: High output can precede full recovery of concentration and electrolyte regulation, so losses still require assessment.
learningObjective: Continue volume and electrolyte assessment when urine output rises during AKI recovery.

title: Monitor potassium after redistribution treatment
stem: A client with kidney failure receives protocol insulin and glucose for hyperkalemia. Potassium initially falls. Why are repeat potassium and glucose checks still needed?
options: The shift may be temporary and treatment can cause hypoglycemia
A lower potassium proves renal elimination has recovered
Only glucose needs follow-up once the rhythm improves
The initial glucose dose prevents every later low glucose
why: Insulin redistributes potassium without directly removing the body's excess.
The fall can occur through redistribution despite persistent kidney failure.
Potassium may rise again while elimination remains impaired.
Hypoglycemia can occur after treatment and requires monitoring.
takeaway: Insulin redistributes potassium without directly removing the body's excess.
learningObjective: Distinguish a temporary intracellular potassium shift from removal of excess body potassium.
